2611.05535.abstract: Compact multi-planet systems orbiting ultracool dwarfs, such as TRAPPIST-1, may be a major population of terrestrial worlds with poorly constrained demographics. Individual close-in planets are expected to escape microlensing detection, but whether a compact system can produce a detectable collective signal remains to be quantified. We calculate the microlensing signal from each TRAPPIST-1 planet, and of all seven combined, if the system were a lens toward the bulge. For a 0.09 $M_\odot$ lens at 4 kpc, $R_E \approx 1.21$ AU, placing the planets at $s = 0.010$--$0.051~\theta_E$, 12--63 times interior to the lensing zone. We measure each signal as the residual after fitting a single-lens model, which accounts for the barycentric dipole. Because the quadrupole term cancels between the two images to first order, the residual scales as the octupole ($q s^3$), reaching $|\delta A / A| \sim 10^{-6}$. The seven planets combined yield $\Delta\chi^2 \sim 10^{-3}$ even at 1~mmag precision, five orders of magnitude below the standard detection threshold. Detection requires increasing all planet masses by a factor of $\sim$300, whereas the resonant chain loses its guarantee of Hill stability at a factor of $\sim$7. Only a lens within $\sim$15 pc of the source or the Sun places the outer planets in the lensing zone. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is therefore not expected to detect a TRAPPIST-1-like system through microlensing, whereas its transit channel in the same fields can detect such planets in large numbers, marking a sharp boundary in the Galactic census between microlensing and transit sensitivity.

2611.05727.abstract: Ganymede is the only Solar System satellite with a global magnetic field driven by a core dynamo. Although its small moment-of-inertia (MoI) factor indicates a differentiated structure of a metallic core, rocky mantle, and outer hydrosphere, its exact bulk composition and layer thicknesses remain highly uncertain. We developed a comprehensive, long-term thermochemical evolution model that couples thermal history with magnetic field generation. Building upon previous theoretical frameworks, this study systematically evaluates how diverse chondritic precursor compositions constrain Ganymede's internal thermochemical evolution and core solidification processes. Based on interior structures initially permitted by a wide range of chondritic compositions and geodetic constraints, we applied the observed equatorial surface magnetic field strength ($\sim$719 nT) as a dynamic filter. Our evolutionary simulations demonstrate that while magnetic dynamos can operate under entire melting, Fe-snow, and FeS-layer regimes, the requirement to sustain the observed field strength strongly restricts the viable interior models. Satisfying this constraint preferentially requires a relatively large core radius and a specific, non-eutectic bulk core sulfur concentration. Consequently, this coupled thermochemical approach highlights the main novelty of this study: characterizing the hydrosphere's density serves as an independent constraint to break the structural degeneracy of Ganymede's bulk composition. Our model indicates that L and CI chondrites yield parameter spaces capable of sustaining comparable field strengths under a low-density hydrosphere scenario (1,200 kg m-3), whereas the H chondrite composition can satisfy this criterion under a high-density scenario (1,300 kg m-3). These predictions provide a critical framework to be tested by the JUICE mission arriving in 2031.

2611.05740.abstract: M dwarf stars represent prime targets for the detection and characterization of small, temperate exoplanets; however, their complex activity and convective surfaces pose significant challenges for high-resolution spectroscopic studies. This work aims to investigate the impact of stellar convection on high-resolution spectroscopic observations of M dwarf stars and develop an integrated approach combining 3D radiative hydrodynamical simulations, spectroscopic modeling, and transit analysis to mitigate stellar noise. We employ 3D radiative hydrodynamical simulations of M dwarf stellar convection to generate synthetic spectra. We compare the synthetic spectra to actual observations of GJ 3470. We model a high-resolution transit sequence of the Neptune-size GJ 3470 b, including centre-to-limb variations (CLVs) and the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect (RME), and process the sequence via principal component analysis (PCA) to de-trend stellar effects. Comparison of synthetic spectra with actual observations shows that current H2O line lists remain inaccurate, with modest agreement in line strength and position for the chosen K-band interval. During the transit of GJ 3470 b, the amplitude of CLVs+RME is comparable to exoplanet signals. Current PCA can in principle de-trend such effects, but its behaviour is highly dependent on the copresence of telluric and planetary signals. While we are able to correctly detect the exoplanet with no evident bias from stellar residuals, this result is limited to a narrow spectral interval and a specific orbital configuration. This study demonstrates that 3D radiative hydrodynamical simulations are essential for accurately modeling convection-induced spectral variability in M dwarfs. Our integrated framework establishes a foundation to obtain unbiased measurements from future ELT observations of exoplanets orbiting M dwarfs.

2611.05963.abstract: Super-Earths are commonly found with cold Jupiters, yet it is unclear whether these Super-Earth-Cold-Jupiter (SE-CJ) systems differ architecturally from other Kepler-like systems (Non-SE-CJ). One might expect the CJs to excite eccentricities and mutual inclinations among the SEs. We use two metrics: the normalized transit duration $T/T_0$, set by the host-star density, and the pairwise duration ratio $\xi$ between neighboring transiting planets. We find no population-level difference in $T/T_0$ between the samples. Forward modeling of $\xi$, which is more directly sensitive to mutual inclinations because it isolates the impact-parameter contrast, finds no evidence that SE-CJ systems are more mutually inclined than Non-SE-CJ systems, and hints they could be even flatter. We infer a Rayleigh dispersion in mutual inclination of $\delta \approx 1.0^\circ$, or a characteristic eccentricity of $e \approx 0.035$ (assuming equipartition), compared with $\delta \approx 1.5^\circ$ and $e \approx 0.05$ for Non-SE-CJ systems. Many SE-CJ systems therefore retain nearly coplanar, low-eccentricity architectures despite hosting distant giants. We further show that secular coupling among the inner Super-Earths usually dominates over forcing from the cold Jupiter, leaving the inner planets resistant to excitation. Our analysis is limited to SE-CJ systems with multiple transiting SEs: systems in which the CJ has strongly excited the inner architecture are expected to present as single-transiting, and cannot be studied with the $\xi$ metric. Another caveat of our result is that undetected cold Jupiters in the comparison sample could dilute the measured $\xi$ distribution.

2611.06765.abstract: Tidal interactions between planets and discs modify semimajor axes and eccentricities. These effects are represented by migration and eccentricity damping timescales in analytical and Nbody models, although they are assumed constant. This approximation is uncertain in resonant multiplanet systems, where coupled planet disc evolution can produce non-linear torque feedback. We investigate migration and eccentricity damping in two planet systems undergoing resonant and overstable evolution near the 2:1 mean motion resonance. Using hydrodynamic simulations with varying disc surface densities, viscosities, and aspect ratios, we measure both timescales from energy and angular momentum exchange between the planets and disc. We find that both timescales are time dependent and vary throughout the evolution. In resonant systems, sign reversals occur owing to eccentricity oscillations and disc torque variations. Moreover, migration timescales normalised by their expected dependence on planetary mass, disc surface density, and aspect ratio deviate between models. Likewise, the common relation between migration and eccentricity damping timescales is not recovered. We compare the hydrodynamic evolution with several Nbody approaches. Models with constant migration and damping timescales fail to reproduce the hydrodynamic evolution, whereas torque-based approaches provide better agreement. In particular, approaches including corotation torque saturation and planetary eccentricity reproduce the hydrodynamic evolution in the type I migration regime, whereas additional corrections are required when planets partially open gaps. These results show that time-dependent torque-based prescriptions provide a consistent physical link between hydrodynamic simulations and simplified Nbody models of resonant planetary systems.

2611.06915.abstract: Gaia's fourth data release (DR4) will provide epoch astrometry for billions of sources, enabling the detection of potentially tens of thousands of substellar companions. We present the epochalypse catalog: Gaia DR4-like epoch astrometry for testing orbit-modeling pipelines on a common set of injected systems with known parameters. Onto each of the $5{,}040{,}328$ main-sequence Gaia stars within $500\,{ \rm pc}$ in the G23H catalog, we inject a zero-, one-, and two-companions system, for $15{,}120{,}984$ systems in total. Companion masses and semimajor axes are drawn log-uniformly over $1\,M_{ \rm Mars}$--$80\,M_{ \rm Jup}$ and $0.03$--$100\,{ \rm au}$, with no occurrence model and no detectability cut, so orbital periods extend well beyond the mission baseline and the companion-free population serves as a matched null. We also flag sub-populations of one- and two-companions systems whose companions are potentially detectable, based on an estimated signal-to-noise ratio that accounts for each star's noise, number of transits, and the suppression of signals with periods longer than the baseline. As a demonstration, we run the kepmodel astrometric periodogram on every system and find that signal detection and period localization decouple beyond the DR4 baseline: long-period companions can produce significant astrometric curvature while their periods, and therefore their masses, remain poorly constrained. Under any companion occurrence model, this population of systems where the orbit is detectable but not characterizable will far outnumber the population with fully characterizable orbits. The epochalypse catalog, its full generation pipeline, and a modeling tutorial are publicly available.

2611.05435.title: From Earth's Harshest Landscapes to Lunar Horizons: Engineering NEA Telescopes for Extreme Environments

figures.caption: Figure 1: Orbital distribution of some known near-Earth objects and selected spacecraft missions for asteroid and comet exploration.
Figure 2: Global distribution of the AMAS (Atacama–Mongolia–Antarctica–Sahara) test sites forming a distributed terrestrial analog network for validating technologies for future lunar observatories.

Figure 3: The proposed architecture assumes a protected and autonomous observatory environment in which optical instruments operate within a controlled enclosure. The use of transparent protective structures, re-purposed mirrors (or segmented mirrors) from previous space missions introduces additional engineering challenges, including optical alignment, wavefront control, and thermal stability. These challenges represent key technology developments required for future lunar observatories.

Figure 4: Conceptual architecture of a future Earth–Moon planetary defence network. Ground-based observatories, lunar survey telescopes, infrared monitoring stations, autonomous processing pipelines, and AI-assisted risk assessment systems operate as a coordinated global infrastructure for Near-Earth Object detection and early warning.

2611.05435.abstract: Near-Earth Asteroids (NEAs) represent both a scientific opportunity and a potential threat to human civilization. While current survey programs have successfully detected most large NEAs, a significant observational gap remains for objects smaller than approximately 140 m, which can still produce regional-scale devastation. Ground-based surveys are intrinsically limited by atmospheric conditions, weather, and solar avoidance constraints, which leave a significant fraction of near-Sun objects difficult to detect. In particular, Earth-based observatories remain largely blind to objects approaching from the Sun-ward direction, reducing available warning times. Future lunar observatories offer a promising solution to this limitation. A telescope operating on the Moon could enable observations of regions inaccessible from Earth, provide enhanced sensitivity, and significantly improve early detection capabilities. However, the lunar environment imposes severe engineering constraints, including thermal cycling, dust contamination, radiation exposure, and autonomous operation requirements. We propose the AMAS(Atacama-Mongolia-Antarctica-Sahara) project, an international initiative using Earth's most extreme environments as analogue sites for future lunar astronomical facilities. By deploying and testing specialized NEA survey telescopes in these environments, key technologies for future lunar observatories can be validated under realistic operational conditions. This paper presents the scientific rationale, engineering challenges, site selection strategy, and long-term roadmap toward a global Earth-Moon network for planetary defense.

2611.06549.title: Population synthesis of substellar companions surviving common-envelope evolution

figures.caption: Figure 1: Stellar-radius evolution showing the thermal-pulse classification for a progenitor with initial mass $2.041\,M_{\odot}$ and metallicity $Z=0.0112$. Radial responses to thermal pulses during the TP-AGB (a). A zoom-in of a radial response showing the thermal cycle associated with one pulse, including the surrounding interpulse evolution (b). The expansion toward the maximum stellar radius and the later contraction (c). The light-orange region marks the radial-pulse window. The dark-orange region marks the Near-$R_{\rm max}$ interval, defined as $\pm 10\%$ of the radial-window duration around $t(R_{\rm max})$.

Figure 2: CE outcomes as a function of evolutionary stage at CE onset for the 295 analyzed systems. Panels (a) and (b) show the $E_{\rm pot}+E_{\rm therm}$ and $E_{\rm pot}+E_{\rm int}$ prescriptions, respectively, for $\alpha_{\rm CE}=0.3$. Panels (c) and (d) show the corresponding prescriptions for $\alpha_{\rm CE}=1$. Red, blue, and gray regions represent mergers, survivors, and indeterminate systems with $E_{\rm bind}\geq 0$, respectively. While more systems survive when recombination energy is included, even without this additional energy, some planets can survive if CE evolution starts with the host star on the late AGB.

Figure 3: Orbital and stellar evolution of a 9.39 MJ survivor that enters CE evolution near the maximum stellar radius under the $E_{\rm pot}+E_{\rm therm}$ prescription with $\alpha_{\rm CE}=1$. The left panel shows the host-star evolution from the RGB through the AGB, while the right panel shows a zoom-in of the TP-AGB pulses around CE onset, with the contact region enlarged in the inset. Red, blue, and green curves show the stellar radius, the periastron stellar Roche-lobe radius, and the orbital periastron distance, respectively. Orbital tracks terminate at contact, therefore the dashed red curve is the continuation of the undisturbed stellar track. The shaded orange 100 yr interval shows the fixed-structure approximation adopted in Sect. 2.2, rather than a CE duration calculated for this system. The survivor shows the importance of the evolutionary stage at CE onset, in particular during a thermal pulse where even a low-mass companion can survive without recombination energy.

Figure 4: CE outcomes as a function of initial conditions of the 295 systems. Panels (a) and (b) show the initial eccentricity versus the initial orbital separation in au, for the $E_{\rm pot}+E_{\rm therm}$ and $E_{\rm pot}+E_{\rm int}$ prescriptions, respectively. Panels (c) and (d) show companion mass versus the initial periastron distance for the same two prescriptions. Red crosses indicate mergers at both adopted CE efficiencies. Orange triangles represent survival only for $\alpha_{\rm CE}=1$. Blue circles indicate survival at $\alpha_{\rm CE}=0.3$. Gray diamonds represent indeterminate systems with $E_{\rm bind}\geq 0$. No single property determines survival alone. While wider initial orbits and higher companion masses favor survival, even without including recombination energy, planets with masses as low as $\sim 9.39$ MJ can survive if CE evolution starts when the host star is close to the maximum radius during a thermal pulse.

Figure 5: Normalized distributions of progenitor masses (a) and WD-mass estimates (b) for the $E_{\rm pot}+E_{\rm int}$ prescription with $\alpha_{\rm CE}=1$. Each histogram is normalized to unit area. Vertical dashed lines mark the median of each population. The seven indeterminate systems are shown individually as tick marks along the x-axis. Survivor WD masses are approximated by the core masses at CE onset. For merging and indeterminate systems, we used WD masses corresponding to single-star evolution. Survivors tend to originate from higher-mass progenitors but have lower estimated WD masses because CE ejection terminates subsequent core growth.

Figure 6: Companion masses and final orbital periods of post-CE survivors. Orange triangles represent the $E_{\rm pot}+E_{\rm therm}$ prescription with $\alpha_{\rm CE}=1$. Blue circles and green squares represent the $E_{\rm pot}+E_{\rm int}$ prescription with $\alpha_{\rm CE}=0.3$ and 1, respectively. The upper axis provides an approximate final semimajor axis using Kepler’s third law with the median core and companion masses of all survivors, $\tilde{M}_{\rm c}=0.574\,M_{\odot}$ and $\tilde{M}_{p}=0.0216\,M_{\odot}$ (22.693 MJ), respectively. The red dashed curve marks the onset of companion RLOF, calculated using the Eggleton approximation and the median core mass quoted above. Most survivors have orbital periods of a few hours. However, including the full internal energy during CE evolution permits substantially wider final orbits.

Figure 7: Predicted transit-detection probabilities for post-CE survivors at a TESS-like cadence of 120 s. Gray crosses represent the geometric probability, $p_{\rm transit}$, while symbols show $p_{\rm detection}$. Orange triangles represent the $E_{\rm pot}+E_{\rm therm}$ prescription with $\alpha_{\rm CE}=1$. Blue circles and green squares represent the $E_{\rm pot}+E_{\rm int}$ prescription with $\alpha_{\rm CE}=0.3$ and 1, respectively. Error bars show 95% Wilson confidence intervals (Wilson 1927) on the injection-recovery sensitivity propagated to $p_{\rm detection}$. The simulations assume a continuous 27.4-d baseline and Gaussian white noise normalized to 1% RMS in one hour. As expected, the detection probabilities lie close to the geometric transit probabilities, indicating that orbital orientation is the main limitation.

Figure 8: Top: Spectral energy distribution of one of our systems, showing the WD (blue), the companion (red), and their combined emission (black dashed curve). The horizontal bars indicate the half-power wavelength ranges of the MIRI filters, as reported in the JWST documentation. The WD parameters are $M_{\mathrm{WD}}=0.61\,M_{\odot}$, $T_{\mathrm{WD}}=5439$ K, and $t_{\mathrm{cooling}}=3.74$ Gyr, while the companion is a planet with $M_{\mathrm{p}}=9.4\,M_{\mathrm{J}}$, $T_{\mathrm{p}}=386$ K, and $a_{\mathrm{f}}=0.006\,{\mathrm{au}}$. Bottom: Infrared excess, expressed as the ratio of the planetary flux to the WD flux. Despite the companion’s relatively modest mass, well within the planetary regime, its proximity to the WD results in a higher effective temperature, producing a significant infrared excess at wavelengths beyond $8\,\mu\mathrm{m}$.

2611.06549.abstract: Predicting the population of substellar companions around white dwarfs (WDs) requires accounting for both companions that avoid engulfment during stellar evolution and those that survive common-envelope (CE) evolution. While the former population was investigated in our previous population-synthesis study, a comprehensive population synthesis of the latter remains lacking. We investigated the fate of engulfed substellar companions within the same population-synthesis framework. We aim to predict the occurrence rates and properties of companions surviving CE evolution, identify the conditions permitting survival, and assess their detectability. We determined the stellar structure at the onset of CE evolution and calculated CE outcomes for different ejection efficiencies considering gravitational and thermal energy or the full internal energy of the envelope. Survival is rare and strongly depends on the evolutionary stage at engulfment. No companions entering CE evolution during the red-giant branch or early asymptotic-giant branch survive. Survivors originate exclusively from the thermally pulsing asymptotic-giant branch, when stellar envelopes can become weakly bound, allowing even relatively low-mass companions to survive. The resulting systems typically have orbital periods of a few hours. We predict occurrence rates of up to 0.16% among WDs, corresponding to an upper limit of 2.53 companions to WDs within 50 pc. Transit detection is primarily limited by orbital geometry, whereas all predicted survivors would produce detectable infrared excess with JWST out to 50pc. We predict that CE evolution produces a small but observable population of close substellar companions to WDs. Survival is governed not only by companion mass but critically by the envelope structure at engulfment, particularly during thermal pulses, and by the contribution of recombination energy to envelope ejection.
